html:
The Pankararu are an Indigenous people of the dry backlands of Pernambuco in north-eastern Brazil, near the São Francisco River. Their own language, probably an isolate, has died out, and today they speak Portuguese.

The north-east was the first part of Portuguese Brazil to be colonised, and its peoples faced cattle ranchers, missions and wars from the 1600s. In the 1700s and 1800s the Pankararu were gathered at a mission at Brejo dos Padres, where most still live. They kept their identity through rituals such as the Toré dance and the masked Praiá dancers. Like many north-eastern peoples, they won official recognition from the Brazilian state in the 1900s. See also Puri, another eastern people of Brazil.
